translations: The lantern's flame still flickered, the water jug's surface remained calm like a mirror, and the guai tree's branches swayed gently in the breeze without any new cracks appearing. Wu Gang stood beneath the tree, his gaze shifting from initial arrogance to a quiet introspection, as if he had found a solitary reflection in the repetition of chopping and healing.
Aman carefully stored the bamboo slips and whispered softly

He truly had a knack for it. He could quickly memorize the phrases he'd heard and make a rough approximation of new techniques. Because he learned so fast, he didn't want to linger on the same thing, and as soon as he saw repetition, he thought he already understood.

One time, he tried to prove himself by doing everything at once – carrying water jugs on his shoulders, reciting the star poem, and practicing wind control in his feet. When the mountain wind changed direction, the left jug spilled most of its water, the right jug crashed into the stone wall, and he got the star poem wrong.
Aman helped him straighten the empty jug, simply recording the results without helping him refill the water. Wu Gang still said he would be able to handle it all next time.
The immortal master finally warned, "Knowing many things isn't wrong, but abandoning it halfway is. Cultivating oneself isn't about piling up many beginnings."

Wu Gang nodded, but only remembered the first half of the phrase "Knowing many things isn't wrong." He finally filled the water jug, and because of that, he thought he had proven he could continue learning new techniques.

The path of entry was still unbroken, but the problem was already clearly revealed: Wu Gang truly sought immortality, and he was willing to put in the effort, but he only loved new and quick results, and he wasn't willing to finish one thing through slow repetition. This lack of focus would soon turn from a joke to a mistake that would affect his fellow disciples.
The next time the disciples needed to practice alchemy, one person had to guard the furnace alone.

The materials in the furnace had been collected by the disciples for a long time, and the fire couldn't be suddenly high or low, nor could it be interrupted in the middle of the night. The immortal master assigned the task to Wu Gang, clearly stating that he only needed to guard the furnace that night and not practice any other techniques.

Wu Gang promised to do so. He added fuel to the fire and kept an eye on it, initially being very focused. In the first half of the night, the flames were stable, and the furnace produced a uniform, gentle sound. He gradually felt that guarding the furnace was not that difficult, and continuing to sit there was a waste of his talents.

A sudden wind blew from outside the mountain. A fellow disciple mentioned that a fellow immortal was demonstrating wind control tonight, and missing it would mean waiting a long time. Wu Gang thought that leaving for just a moment wouldn't affect the furnace, so he asked a passing disciple to take his place and rushed to the neighboring peak.
Aman was recording the guard duty outside the furnace room, blocking Wu Gang's path and asking, "The immortal master said you couldn't leave."
"I'll just take a quick look and come back."
"You said the same thing last time when you were carrying water."
"This time it's close by."
Aman didn't have the authority to tie Wu Gang to the furnace, but he wrote down the time and place of Wu Gang's departure on the bamboo slips.

The wind control demonstration was even more impressive than Wu Gang had imagined. He watched the first technique and thought the second one was the key; he watched the second technique and wanted to know how to land it. By the time he rushed back, the furnace fire had shifted to one side, and the substitute guardian was anxious, adding more fuel.

Wu Gang was afraid of being discovered, so he immediately used the half-learned wind control technique to fan the flames. The wind was too strong, and the fire suddenly rose high, causing the furnace lid to shake. The fellow disciples hastily retreated, and the previously prepared materials were ruined due to uneven heating.

The immortal master arrived to stabilize the furnace fire, preventing the accident from getting worse. The materials collected over many years couldn't be recovered, and this batch of alchemy had to be stopped.

Wu Gang initially tried to justify himself, saying he had left for only a short time and someone else had taken his place; he also said that if he had mastered wind control, he could have made up for it. The immortal master asked him, "Why do you always blame it on not knowing more, rather than wondering why you didn't keep your promise to guard the furnace?"
Wu Gang was silent.

The fellow disciples didn't scold him, but instead carefully collected the unused materials, one by one. Someone had been waiting for a certain mountain grass for several seasons, but now they would have to start over. Wu Gang saw for the first time that seeking quick results not only left him empty-handed but also wasted other people's time.
He volunteered to clean up the furnace room and apologized to the fellow disciples. Aman recorded the apology, but didn't erase the previous note about Wu Gang's unauthorized departure.
"Wouldn't a sincere apology make up for it?" Wu Gang asked.
"Things that have happened can't be erased by a later apology," Aman said. "The bamboo slips are like that, and the furnace is probably the same."

Wu Gang didn't argue this time. He spent several nights guarding a newly lit furnace, learning to recognize the subtle changes each time. However, in his heart, he still had a thought: if he could find a truly exceptional shortcut, he could make up for all his losses and prove that he wasn't incapable of focus, but that his previous methods were just too slow.

His goal of seeking immortality hadn't changed, but his approach was still avoiding the most basic aspect of guarding. Wu Gang considered "finding a faster method" to be progress, and therefore couldn't see that he was using a new excuse to avoid the same task.

The immortal master saw that he still didn't understand, so he took away all the side techniques and left only a new furnace. The furnace contained precious materials that had been re-collected, and they needed to be allowed to develop naturally and slowly. If Wu Gang could guard the furnace from start to finish, the immortal master would consider letting him continue his training; if he made any changes again, he would have to face the consequences.

Aman gently closed the bamboo slips, drawing a thin line on the back of the paper with her finger, as if marking the end of this silent test. She didn't linger by the furnace or make a joke about Wu Gang, like "Don't forget to tighten the lid," because such lighthearted teasing had lost its resonance in the quiet moon palace.
